product_description: Hand felted pure wool namda wall hanging made from original sheep wool. It has one pocket. This hanging is handmade using Namda process, a rare and unique craft originating in the Mughal era, wherein splendid floor pieces are made from 100% sheep wool (white or dyed) by practice of felting the wool rather than weaving it. The mat is then rolled tightly and tied up with a rope and compressed by way of rolling to-and-fro on the floor with the help of hands and feet for about an hour which allows fusing together of the fibre technically known as 'fibre to fibre' fusion. The rope is then untied, and the mat unrolled to discover the well-shaped Namda.

product_description: Beautifully handcrafted Rajasthani couple bobble head puppet / kathputli. In Rajasthan the puppet tradition is called Kathputli, where Kaath means wood and Putli means Puppet. Kathputli means a puppet made out of wood. However Kathputlis typically have wooden torso and shoulders while the legs (absent in the ones based on a female character) and arms are made of clothes stuffed with cotton. Kathputli’s are string puppets controlled by strings which passes from the top of the puppets and manipulated by the puppeteer. These highly decorative handmade puppets are the source of age old tradition of narration of historical stories, myths and legends. The narrations were accompanied with music and dialogues delivered by the group members. Kathputli became one of the most important and well know performing arts of Rajasthan and it represents the tradition, customs and socio-cultural backdrop of the state.

product_title: Multicolor - Handpainted Tholu Bommalata Leather Necklace
product_description: Fine multicolor handcrafted Tholu Bommalata leather necklace with wooden beads.Tholu Bommalata is the shadow puppet theatre tradition of the state of Andhra Pradesh in India. Tholu bommalata literally means "the dance of leather puppets" (tholu – "leather" and bommalata – "puppet dance") is a 2000 year old craft and is one of the oldest form of performing arts.. The traditional process of crafting shadow puppets requires 30-40 days, from the procurement of leather to the completion of the product. Two other kinds of shadow puppetry are practiced in Andhra Pradesh, the Sutram Bommalata (String puppets) and the Koyya Bommalata(Wooden puppets). The leather puppets, because of their transparency and jewel like glow, are most popular. The puppets are mounted in the middle on a palm stem, extended to form a handle used to move the body of the puppet. The puppets are painted with hands using natural and poster colours. But apart from the translucency and vivid colours, what gives these puppets their brilliance, is the perforated designs drawn on the characters to depict jewellery. Once surrounded by colour and viewed against the light, they look like glowing jewels.

product_description: Fine multicolor handcrafted Tholu Bommalata leather necklace with wooden beads.Tholu Bommalata is the shadow puppet theatre tradition of the state of Andhra Pradesh in India. The traditional process of crafting shadow puppets requires 30-40 days, from the procurement of leather to the completion of the product. Two other kinds of shadow puppetry are practiced in Andhra Pradesh, the Sutram Bommalata (String puppets) and the Koyya Bommalata(Wooden puppets). The leather puppets, because of their transparency and jewel like glow, are most popular. The puppets are mounted in the middle on a palm stem, extended to form a handle used to move the body of the puppet. The puppets are painted with hands using natural and poster colours. But apart from the translucency and vivid colours, what gives these puppets their brilliance, is the perforated designs drawn on the characters to depict jewellery. product_title: Handpainted Tholu Bommalata Leather Earrings
product_description: Fine handcrafted Tholu Bommalata leather earrings.Tholu Bommalata is the shadow puppet theatre tradition of the state of Andhra Pradesh in India. Tholu bommalata literally means "the dance of leather puppets" (tholu – "leather" and bommalata – "puppet dance") is a 2000 year old craft and is one of the oldest form of performing arts.. The traditional process of crafting shadow puppets requires 30-40 days, from the procurement of leather to the completion of the product. Two other kinds of shadow puppetry are practiced in Andhra Pradesh, the Sutram Bommalata (String puppets) and the Koyya Bommalata(Wooden puppets). The leather puppets, because of their transparency and jewel like glow, are most popular. The puppets are mounted in the middle on a palm stem, extended to form a handle used to move the body of the puppet. The puppets are painted with hands using natural and poster colours. But apart from the translucency and vivid colours, what gives these puppets their brilliance, is the perforated designs drawn on the characters to depict jewellery. Once surrounded by colour and viewed against the light, they look like glowing jewels.

product_title: Multicolor - Handpainted Tholu Bommalata Leather Earrings
product_description: Fine multicolor handcrafted Tholu Bommalata leather earrings.Tholu Bommalata is the shadow puppet theatre tradition of the state of Andhra Pradesh in India. Tholu bommalata literally means "the dance of leather puppets" (tholu – "leather" and bommalata – "puppet dance") is a 2000 year old craft and is one of the oldest form of performing arts.. The traditional process of crafting shadow puppets requires 30-40 days, from the procurement of leather to the completion of the product. Two other kinds of shadow puppetry are practiced in Andhra Pradesh, the Sutram Bommalata (String puppets) and the Koyya Bommalata(Wooden puppets). The leather puppets, because of their transparency and jewel like glow, are most popular. The puppets are mounted in the middle on a palm stem, extended to form a handle used to move the body of the puppet. The puppets are painted with hands using natural and poster colours. But apart from the translucency and vivid colours, what gives these puppets their brilliance, is the perforated designs drawn on the characters to depict jewellery. Once surrounded by colour and viewed against the light, they look like glowing jewels.

product_title: Beige - Hakoba Hand Block Ajrakh Print Natural Dyed Cotton Fabric 154
product_description:
Beige hakoba cutwork embroidered ajrakh cotton fabric is crafted using natural-dyeing and resist block-printing techniques. This ancient craft is estimated to be around 4,500 years old. The Ajrakh artisans in India originally migrated from Sindh to the Kutch region of Gujarat and to Barmer in Rajasthan. Ajrakh is also the traditional attire of the Maldhari pastoral & khatri community of Bhuj Gujarat. The process is long and detailed, involving multiple stages where each layer of colour is printed only after a resting period, allowing the cloth to absorb the dye fully. Made from pure cotton, it is ideal for creating kurtas, shirts, dresses or even home decor items.

Each piece is hand block printed and dyed using natural colors over a slow process of 15–20 days. As a result, you may notice slight variations in color, mild pigment smudges or irregular dye patterns, these are not defects. Black hakoba cutwork embroidered ajrakh cotton fabric is crafted using natural-dyeing and resist block-printing techniques. This ancient craft is estimated to be around 4,500 years old. Ajrakh is also the traditional attire of the Maldhari pastoral & khatri community of Bhuj Gujarat. The process is long and detailed, involving multiple stages where each layer of colour is printed only after a resting period, allowing the cloth to absorb the dye fully. Made from pure cotton, it is ideal for creating kurtas, shirts, dresses or even home decor items.
A Note on Handmade Beauty
Each piece is hand block printed and dyed using natural colors over a slow process of 15–20 days. As a result, you may notice slight variations in color, mild pigment smudges or irregular dye patterns, these are not defects. Black hakoba cutwork embroidered ajrakh cotton fabric is crafted using natural-dyeing and resist block-printing techniques. This ancient craft is estimated to be around 4,500 years old. The Ajrakh artisans in India originally migrated from Sindh to the Kutch region of Gujarat and to Barmer in Rajasthan. Ajrakh is also the traditional attire of the Maldhari pastoral & khatri community of Bhuj Gujarat. The process is long and detailed, involving multiple stages where each layer of colour is printed only after a resting period, allowing the cloth to absorb the dye fully. Made from pure cotton, it is ideal for creating kurtas, shirts, dresses or even home decor items.
A Note on Handmade Beauty
Each piece is hand block printed and dyed using natural colors over a slow process of 15–20 days. As a result, you may notice slight variations in color, mild pigment smudges or irregular dye patterns, these are not defects. They’re gentle marks of authenticity, proudly bearing the touch of human hands, heritage, and nature’s own palette. Wear them like a signature, because no two pieces are ever alike.

Authentic brown hand block batik print pure handwoven natural dyed kala cotton fabric by Khamir, Kutch celebrates the centuries old batik tradition of Kutch, believed to have travelled to the region during the Ramayana era through skilled master craftsmen. Practised by the Khatri community, Batik became an important textile art of Kutch and was widely exported from Mandvi port to Indonesia since the 1500s. This fabric is created using the traditional wax-resist block printing technique, where heated wax is applied with intricately carved wooden blocks before dyeing. The wax resists colour, forming delicate vein-like and webbed patterns unique to batik. Repeated waxing, dyeing and washing create layered motifs and rich depth, making the fabric suitable for ethnic wear, contemporary outfits and home decor creations.
A Note on Handmade Beauty
Each piece is hand block printed and dyed using natural colors over a slow process of 15–20 days. As a result, you may notice slight variations in color, mild pigment smudges, or irregular dye patterns, these are not defects. They’re gentle marks of authenticity, proudly bearing the touch of human hands, heritage, and nature’s own palette. Wear them like a signature, because no two pieces are ever alike.

product_title: Hakoba Hand Block Ajrakh Print Natural Dyed Cotton Fabric 104
product_description:
Hakoba cutwork embroidered ajrakh cotton fabric is crafted using natural-dyeing and resist block-printing techniques. This ancient craft is estimated to be around 4,500 years old. The Ajrakh artisans in India originally migrated from Sindh to the Kutch region of Gujarat and to Barmer in Rajasthan. Ajrakh is also the traditional attire of the Maldhari pastoral & khatri community of Bhuj Gujarat. The process is long and detailed, involving multiple stages where each layer of colour is printed only after a resting period, allowing the cloth to absorb the dye fully. Made from pure cotton, it is ideal for creating kurtas, shirts, dresses or even home decor items.
A Note on Handmade Beauty
Each piece is hand block printed and dyed using natural colors over a slow process of 15–20 days. As a result, you may notice slight variations in color, mild pigment smudges or irregular dye patterns, these are not defects. They’re gentle marks of authenticity, proudly bearing the touch of human hands, heritage, and nature’s own palette. Wear them like a signature, because no two pieces are ever alike.

product_title: Black - Kutch Hand Block Ajrakh Print Natural Dyed Cotton Fabric 01
product_description:
Black ajrakh hand block print natural dyed cotton fabric is carefully crafted by master artisan Jabbar Khatri from Kutch, Gujarat. This ancient craft is believed to be over 4,500 years old, with Ajrakh artisans originally migrating from Sindh to the Kutch region of Gujarat and Barmer in Rajasthan. Ajrakh is also the traditional attire of the Maldhari pastoral community of Bhuj. The process is intricate and time-consuming, involving multiple stages where each layer of colour is printed only after a resting period, it beautifully reflects rich cultural artistry and is ideal for making outfits or home decor items.
A Note on Handmade Beauty
Each piece is hand block printed and dyed using natural colors over a slow process of 15–20 days. As a result, you may notice slight variations in color, mild pigment smudges or irregular dye patterns, these are not defects. They’re gentle marks of authenticity, proudly bearing the touch of human hands, heritage, and nature’s own palette. Wear them like a signature, because no two pieces are ever alike.

Pashmina comes from the Persian word pashmineh, which means made from Pashm or wool in Persian. The wool for Pashmina weaving comes from a distinct breed of goats which are found at an altitude of above 14000 feet in the plateau of Changthan in Ladkah. The goats get their name from the region and are locally known as Changthangi and the wool produced by these goats is called Pashmina. Pashmina fibres are fine and thin, 12-15 microns, ideal for making light weight apparel like fine scarves and shawls. Typically, a goat produces 250- 300 grams of Pashmina per season, comprising 60% fibre and 40% hair. This wool is collected every spring and cleaned before the goat grows a new coat each winter. Pashmina yarn is very fragile and that is why pure pashmina can only be woven with delicate hands on handloom. Weaving is done with a shuttle, carrying the soft Pashmina yarn through the fine yet strong warp. The weaving process is an art that is passed down over generations. It takes about a week to weave a single Pashmina stole.

Pashmina comes from the Persian word pashmineh, which means made from Pashm or wool in Persian. The wool for Pashmina weaving comes from a distinct breed of goats which are found at an altitude of above 14000 feet in the plateau of Changthan in Ladkah. Pashmina fibres are fine and thin, 12-15 microns, ideal for making light weight apparel like fine scarves and shawls. Pashmina yarn is very fragile and that is why pure pashmina can only be woven with delicate hands on handloom. product_title: Black - Mata Ni Pachedi Handpainted Natural Dyed Chanderi Silk Handloom Dupatta 19
product_description:
Black mata ni pachedi handpainted natural dyed chanderi silk handloom dupatta is handpainted by Dilip Chitara of Gujarat using a bamboo stick kalam and Khajuri tree brushes through the Ghasuni process. Colours are mixed with gum to settle into the fabric: haldi for yellow, iron and jaggery for black, imli seeds and fitkari for red, indigo for blue, manjistha root for pink and iron and water for off white. After painting, the dupatta is kept in sunlight for a full day to fix the colours, then washed once to remove any excess. Made from 2/74 mercerised cotton warp and 2/65 chanderi silk weft. Mata ni Pachedi is also called the Kalamkari of Gujarat, thanks to its resemblance to Kalamkari from South India and the same method of painting using a bamboo kalam. Mata ni Pachedi literally means behind the mother goddess. When people of the nomadic Vaghari community of Gujarat were barred from entering temples, they made their own shrines with depictions of the Mother Goddess on cloth. This sacred art, now revered by all, is over 700 years old. Ideal for religious occasions, festive wear and everyday ethnic draping.

Yellow mata ni pachedi handpainted natural dyed chanderi silk handloom dupatta is handpainted by Dilip Chitara of Gujarat using a bamboo stick kalam and Khajuri tree brushes through the Ghasuni process. Colours are mixed with gum to settle into the fabric: haldi for yellow, iron and jaggery for black, imli seeds and fitkari for red, indigo for blue, manjistha root for pink and iron and water for off white. After painting, the dupatta is kept in sunlight for a full day to fix the colours, then washed once to remove any excess. Made from 2/74 mercerised cotton warp and 2/65 chanderi silk weft. Mata ni Pachedi is also called the Kalamkari of Gujarat, thanks to its resemblance to Kalamkari from South India and the same method of painting using a bamboo kalam. Mata ni Pachedi literally means behind the mother goddess. When people of the nomadic Vaghari community of Gujarat were barred from entering temples, they made their own shrines with depictions of the Mother Goddess on cloth. This sacred art, now revered by all, is over 700 years old. Ideal for religious occasions, festive wear and everyday ethnic draping.
